questions.concept: Why Bohr's model had to be replaced
questions.question: Bohr's model predicts hydrogen's spectrum perfectly but fails for helium. What assumption breaks down?
questions.solution: Bohr treats electrons as particles in fixed circular orbits and ignores their WAVE nature and electron–electron interactions. With two electrons, mutual repulsion and wave behaviour (orbital shapes, not circular tracks) dominate — the orbit picture collapses. Schrödinger's wave model replaces orbits with probability orbitals.

questions.question: Distinguish an orbit from an orbital in one sentence each, and say which is a quantum-mechanical concept.
questions.solution: Orbit: a definite circular PATH (Bohr) — the electron is supposed to be there. Orbital: a 3D PROBABILITY region (quantum mechanics) — the shape where the electron is most likely to be found. Only the orbital is a real quantum concept; the orbit violates the uncertainty principle by specifying both position and momentum.

questions.question: State what each of the four quantum numbers specifies, and show that n = 2 can hold 8 electrons.
questions.solution: n (1,2,3…) = shell/energy level; l (0…n−1) = subshell shape (s, p, d, f); m_l (−l…+l) = orbital orientation; m_s (±½) = spin. For n = 2: l = 0 (one s orbital, 2 electrons) + l = 1 (three p orbitals × 2 = 6 electrons) → 2 + 6 = 8. Each orbital holds exactly 2 electrons of opposite spin (Pauli).

questions.concept: Hund's rule — why electrons spread out
questions.question: Why does nitrogen's configuration write 2p³ as ↑ ↑ ↑ (three separate orbitals) rather than pairing two electrons in one p orbital?
questions.solution: Hund's rule: electrons enter degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals singly with parallel spins first. Reason: pairing costs energy (electrostatic repulsion), and parallel spins in separate orbitals also gain exchange energy. Spreading out is lower energy — pairing happens only after every orbital in the subshell has one electron.

questions.question: Why is chromium [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ instead of the expected [Ar]3d⁴4s²?
questions.solution: Half-filled (d⁵) and fully-filled (d¹⁰) subshells have extra stability: symmetric electron distribution and maximum exchange energy. Moving one 4s electron into 3d achieves a half-filled d⁵ — the exchange-energy gain outweighs the cost of the promotion. Cr and Cu are the standard exceptions the rule predicts.

questions.concept: Why spectra are lines, not bands
questions.question: An excited hydrogen atom emits a few sharp lines rather than a continuous band. What does that prove about atomic energy?
questions.solution: Energy levels are QUANTISED, so transitions occur only between fixed levels. Each allowed jump corresponds to one photon energy hν = ΔE and hence one wavelength — a line. A continuum would imply any energy is allowed. Sharp lines are direct evidence for discrete atomic states.

questions.concept: Why Bohr's model had to be replaced
questions.question: Bohr's model predicts the hydrogen spectrum brilliantly, yet it is now abandoned. Give two failures and the deeper reason.
questions.solution: (1) It cannot explain multi-electron atoms or the fine structure/Zeeman splitting. (2) It assumes electrons orbit in defined paths with known momentum and position, violating the uncertainty principle. Deeper reason: it is a semi-classical hybrid — quantised rules bolted onto classical orbits — with no justification for the quantisation condition itself. Quantum mechanics replaces orbits with probability distributions.

questions.concept: Why an orbital is not an orbit
questions.question: An electron in a 1s orbital has a spherically symmetric probability distribution with maximum at the nucleus. Where is the electron 'moving' then?
questions.solution: An orbital is a probability amplitude map, not a path. The electron has no defined trajectory, only a distribution of possible positions; the 1s density peaks at the nucleus because that is where the electron is most likely to be FOUND. Orbital ≠ orbit: the first describes likelihood in space, the second an assumed track.
